idiom_name: IterableOps#filter(pred: A => Boolean), collect with a PartialFunction, View for the lazy form
implementation_notes: filter(pred: A => Boolean) is available on every collection and takes the criterion as a first-class function value; collect takes a PartialFunction and is documented as 'filter + map' because it selects the elements on which the function is defined (isDefinedAt) and transforms them, with orElse/andThen composing partial functions into criteria chains. filterNot, partition, collectFirst and filterIsInstance cover the other shapes. Collections are strict, whereas .view gives a lazy View on which filter(pred: A => Boolean) returns a lazy View[A] - the analogue of a Java Stream - so a chained criterion does not materialise intermediate collections. Function types are contravariant in their parameter (Function1[-T, +R]), so a subtype container needs no covariant Filterer indirection; a dedicated filterer type is worth writing only to give criteria names for interop or introspection.
pitfalls: Strict versus lazy: List.filter allocates a new collection, while a view defers evaluation and re-runs the predicate on each traversal (and wrapping an Iterator or LazyList gives a single-shot source).
collect with an over-narrow guard silently drops elements that the reader expects to see mapped - a wrong case pattern looks like a filter bug rather than a match error.

Collection API drift between standard-library versions (2.13 IterableOps/IterableOnceOps, 3.x, deprecated Traversable) changes available operations and deprecation warnings, so cross-building needs the version-appropriate import.
